134.title: Asking for someone absent
134.hook: an angel says, and for you the same, when you pray for someone behind their back (Muslim)
134.howItsDone: Many Muslims make du'a for family, friends and fellow believers by name in their private prayers, without telling them, following the hadith that an angel says 'and for you the same'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hasanah, the short du'a from Surah al-Baqarah. Your line was good here, good there. Did you ask for both? Day one hundred thirty-four.

Being talked about behind your back usually means gossip. A comment in a group chat you weren't supposed to see. A silence when you walk into the room. Now turn it around. Someone you barely think about has been saying your name, quietly, for a long time, asking for good things for you. You never knew. They never told you. There's a hadith about exactly that, and it adds a twist. Someone else is listening. Today: ameen.
screen: `TALKED ABOUT BEHIND YOUR BACK.` → `NOW TURN IT AROUND.` → `SOMEONE ELSE IS LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim reports it from Abu al-Darda', one of the companions. The Prophet ﷺ said: whenever a Muslim makes du'a for his brother in his absence, behind his back, an angel says: ameen, and for you the same. In Arabic, wa laka bi-mithl. And for you, its like. So, the hadith says, the moment you ask for good for someone who can't hear you, the same good is asked for you. Not by you. By an angel. Another version in Muslim adds that an angel is appointed at the person's head for just this purpose. Why does the absence matter? Because there's no credit in it. The other person will never thank you. You can't be doing it to look kind. A report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi, which some scholars grade weak, goes further, saying the du'a answered most quickly is the one made by someone absent for someone absent. The Qur'an itself is full of people asking for others. Ibrahim asks for forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believers. Surah al-Hashr describes later believers asking forgiveness for those who came before them in faith, people they never met. Notice, too, how the hadith is phrased. It isn't a deal offered in advance. It describes what happens: someone goes out of their way for another person, and finds they've been included.
screen: `AN ANGEL SAYS: AND FOR YOU THE SAME.` · `NO CREDIT, NO THANKS.` · `IBRAHIM ASKS FOR HIS PARENTS.` · `YOU FIND YOU'VE BEEN INCLUDED.` · then, large: `WA LAKA BI-MITHL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who'll never know. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Think of someone who has no idea you're thinking of them. A coworker who seems tired. A neighbor you only wave at. Someone you've fallen out with. Hold their face in mind. If you pray, you can ask Allah for one good thing for them, in your own words, silently. If you don't, simply wish them one good thing, as specifically as you can. Don't tell them afterward. Let it stay behind their back. The bell holds the time.
Ameen, so be it: what the hadith says an angel answers whenever you make du'a for someone absent, behind their back, and for you the same.

Your line: and the same for you. Every time someone crosses your mind today, a name in your inbox, a face on the bus, wish them one good thing, silently, and leave it there. Day one hundred thirty-four.

135.title: The times that open
135.hook: in prostration, the last third of the night, between adhan and iqamah, while fasting
135.howItsDone: Some Muslims save their most important du'a for prostration, the last third of the night, the time between the adhan and the iqamah, and the moments before breaking a fast.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ameen, the angel's answer. Your line was and the same for you. Whose name crossed your mind, and did you wish them one good thing? Day one hundred thirty-five.

Every office has one. The manager whose door is technically always open, but everyone knows the good time to ask is Friday afternoon, after lunch, when things are calm. Timing isn't everything, but it's something. This week we've said du'a can be made anywhere, any time, in any words. That's still true. The door is never locked. But the hadith collections also name certain moments when the door is described as especially wide open. Moments people save their biggest asks for. Today: iqamah.
screen: `THE DOOR IS ALWAYS OPEN.` → `BUT SOME MOMENTS ARE WIDER.` → `WHERE PEOPLE SAVE THEIR BIGGEST ASKS.`

segments.voice: Here are four of them. The first you already know from day one hundred five: in prostration. Sahih Muslim reports that the closest a servant is to his Lord is while prostrating, so ask much there. Forehead on the floor, and some Muslims pour their private requests into those few seconds, silently, in their own words. The second is the last third of the night. Bukhari and Muslim report that every night, when the last third remains, our Lord descends to the nearest heaven and says: who is calling on Me, that I may answer? Who is asking of Me, that I may give? Who is seeking forgiveness, that I may forgive? Scholars have long differed on how to understand that descent; many simply accept it without asking how. Either way, the picture is of a question asked in the dark while almost everyone is asleep. It's why some Muslims set an alarm for an hour before dawn. The third is small and ordinary: between the adhan and the iqamah, the call to prayer and the call to stand. Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi report that a du'a made in that gap is not turned back. Those few minutes when people are waiting in the mosque, checking the time, are described as an open door. The fourth is while fasting. Tirmidhi reports that the fasting person's du'a is among those not rejected, and some Muslims make du'a just before breaking the fast at sunset. There are others in the hadith, like an hour on Friday and the traveler's du'a. But notice what these four share. Lowered. Awake while others sleep. Waiting. Hungry. Moments when a person is a little emptier than usual.
screen: `FIRST: IN PROSTRATION.` · `THE LAST THIRD OF THE NIGHT.` · `BETWEEN THE ADHAN AND THE IQAMAH.` · `WHILE FASTING.` · then, large: `A LITTLE EMPTIER THAN USUAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one time this week. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Run through the four in your mind. Face on the floor. The quiet hour before dawn. The waiting minutes before a prayer. The last minute of an empty stomach. Which one could you actually reach this week? Choose one. Picture it: where you'll be, what the room looks like. If you pray, decide now what you'll ask for when you get there. If not, decide what you'll sit quietly with. The bell holds the time.

Iqamah, the call to stand for prayer: the gap between it and the adhan is one of the moments the hadith describe as especially open to du'a, along with prostration, the last third of the night, and the fast.
Your line: knock at the open door. Put the time you chose into your calendar or set an alarm for it now, and keep one question ready for when it comes. Day one hundred thirty-five.

136.title: Before sleep
136.hook: in Your name I die and I live, before lying down (Bukhari)
136.howItsDone: Many Muslims make wudu before bed, lie on the right side, recite the last three surahs and say 'bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya', and on waking praise Allah for giving life again.

segments.voice: Yesterday: iqamah, one of the times that open, from prostration to the hour before dawn. Your line was knock at the open door. Did you choose your time? Day one hundred thirty-six.

Here's the last thing most of us do every day: scroll. Lights off, face lit blue, one more video, one more headline. Then the phone drops, and we're gone. Seven or eight hours when we don't know where we are, can't guard anything, can't answer anyone. It's the most helpless we'll be all day, and we treat it as nothing. This whole week has been about asking. Just ask. A heavy heart. He is near. Good here and there. For the absent. At the open times. It ends at the edge of sleep. Today: before sleep.
screen: `THE LAST THING: ONE MORE VIDEO.` → `THE MOST HELPLESS HOURS.` → `A WEEK OF ASKING ENDS HERE.`

segments.voice: Bukhari reports from the companion Hudhayfah that when the Prophet ﷺ lay down at night, he put his hand under his cheek and said: bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya. In Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. It's very short. And it's striking. It calls sleep a kind of dying. That isn't just poetry. The Qur'an, in Surah az-Zumar, says Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and also takes, in their sleep, the souls that have not died; He keeps the ones whose death is decreed and sends the others back until a set time. Every night, in this picture, is a small rehearsal. You let go of everything, and you're handed back in the morning. So the same hadith gives the waking words too: alhamdulillahi alladhi ahyana ba'da ma amatana wa ilayhin-nushur. Praise be to Allah, who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the rising. The first thought of the day is thanks for being handed back. Around those two lines, the tradition gathers other habits. Many Muslims make wudu before bed, lie on the right side, and recite the last three short surahs, al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas, blowing lightly into cupped hands and passing them over the body, as Bukhari reports the Prophet did. Some add the Verse of the Throne. None of it is long. It takes less time than one more video. And it changes what the last thing is. Not a headline. A name.
screen: `IN YOUR NAME I DIE AND I LIVE.` · `SLEEP AS A SMALL DYING.` · `HANDED BACK IN THE MORNING.` · `WUDU, RIGHT SIDE, THREE SURAHS.` · then, large: `THE LAST THING IS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse it now, and say it before sleeping tonight. Sit or lie back comfortably. Rest one hand under your cheek, or just let your head tip slightly to the right. Let the day go, one breath at a time: the work, the messages, the argument. If you pray, you can say it quietly: bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya, or in English, in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. If not, simply notice how much you're about to let go of, and let it go. Stay heavy and still. The bell holds the time.
Before sleep. The Prophet's words at bedtime: in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live, and on waking, praise for being given life again. Today's word.
Your line: in your name I sleep. Tonight, put the phone down one minute earlier than usual, and make the last thing you think or say a name, not a headline. Day one hundred thirty-six.

137.title: What a mosque is
137.hook: the place of prostration, open for prayer, learning and gathering
137.howItsDone: Muslims gather at the mosque for the five daily prayers and Friday prayer, and for classes, community meals, weddings and funerals; many mosques also welcome visitors.

segments.voice: Yesterday: before sleep, in Your name I die and I live. Your line was in your name I sleep. Was the last thing last night a name, or a headline? Day one hundred thirty-seven.
screen: `BEFORE SLEEP — IN YOUR NAME I SLEEP.`

segments.voice: You've probably driven past one. Maybe a grand building with a dome and a tall minaret. Maybe a converted shop on a strip mall, with a hand-painted sign and a row of shoes visible through the glass door. Maybe a room in a university basement. From the outside, they look nothing alike. And if you're not Muslim, you may never have been inside one, or been sure you'd be allowed. This week, the path walks you through a visit, one step at a time. It starts with the name on the sign. Today: what a mosque is.
screen: `A DOME, A STRIP MALL, A BASEMENT.` → `NEVER BEEN INSIDE?` → `A WEEK-LONG VISIT, STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is masjid. You met its root on day one hundred five: sujud, prostration. A masjid is simply the place of prostration, the place where people put their foreheads on the floor. Notice what the name doesn't require. Not a dome. Not a minaret. Not even a building. Bukhari reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that the whole earth has been made a masjid for him, a place of prayer. That's why you'll see Muslims pray in parks, airports and parking lots. Any clean ground will do. So what makes a building a mosque? Go back to the first ones. When the Prophet arrived in Medina, one of the first things he did was build one, with his own hands alongside the companions, as the reports describe: walls of mud brick, pillars of palm trunks, a roof of palm leaves. And look at what went on inside. The five prayers, of course. But also teaching. And poor companions with nowhere else to go, staying in a sheltered part of the mosque known as the Suffah. Bukhari even reports a tent pitched in the mosque for a wounded companion, so the Prophet could visit him from close by, and, on an Eid, men from Abyssinia putting on a display with their spears, while the Prophet's wife Aisha watched. It was a house of prayer that was also a school, a shelter, a clinic and a town square. Mosques today often carry on the same mix: the five prayers, weekend classes, food drives, weddings, funerals. And some hold open days for visitors who simply want to see.
screen: `MASJID — THE PLACE OF PROSTRATION.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH IS A MASJID.` · `MUD BRICK AND PALM TRUNKS.` · `SCHOOL, SHELTER, CLINIC, SQUARE.` · then, large: `A PLACE TO BOW, AND MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two parts. First, sit, and picture the ground you're on right now, the floor under your chair, the earth under the building. If the whole earth is a place to bow, this spot counts too. Let that settle for a few breaths. Then, when the bell has finished, open a map and look for the nearest mosque. Notice its name, how far it is, whether it's a big building or a small room. You don't have to go. Just know where it is. For now, breathe, and feel the ground. The bell holds the time.
Masjid. A mosque: the place of prostration, open for prayer, learning and gathering. Today's word.
Your line: a place to bow. As you move through today, notice one spot, a park, a quiet corner, the floor of your room, and think: this could be a place to bow. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

138.title: Shoes off, right foot in
138.hook: shoes at the door, enter with the right foot, a greeting prayer on the lips
138.howItsDone: At the mosque, Muslims leave their shoes at the door, step in with the right foot first saying 'Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik', and leave with the left foot, asking Allah for His bounty.

segments.voice: Yesterday: masjid, the place of prostration, and a school, shelter and town square too. Your line was a place to bow. Did you find the nearest mosque on the map? Day one hundred thirty-eight.

A row of shoes by a front door says a lot about a house. A neat rack in a friend's hallway. A basket of slippers. Grandma's mat, where nobody gets past in sneakers. Step out of your shoes and you step out of the outside world, literally, and your feet land on something softer. At a mosque door the pile is bigger: a long shelf, or just a heap, of sneakers, loafers, tiny children's sandals, work boots. That pile is the first thing a visitor meets. Today: shoes off, right foot in.
screen: `SHOES AT GRANDMA'S DOOR.` → `STEPPING OUT OF THE OUTSIDE.` → `A PILE OF SHOES AT THE MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Why shoes off? The simplest answer is the floor. In a mosque, people put their foreheads on that carpet five times a day. You wouldn't walk across a kitchen table in the shoes you wore through a parking lot. So the shoes stay at the door, and the carpet stays clean. It isn't that shoes are forbidden in prayer as such. Bukhari reports that the companion Anas was asked whether the Prophet ﷺ ever prayed in his sandals, and he said yes. Scholars add that the sandals must be clean. But on a shared carpet, shoes off is the custom. Then the right foot. Aisha said, in Bukhari, that the Prophet liked to begin with the right in everything he could: putting on his sandals, combing his hair, washing for prayer. So it's customary to step into the mosque right foot first, and step out left foot first. It's a small thing. It turns an ordinary doorway into a moment you notice. And the words on the lips. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet teaching that on entering the mosque one says: Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik. O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy. And on leaving: O Allah, I ask You for Your bounty. Mercy inside, bounty outside. For a visitor, a few more things help. Modest, loose clothes. Mosques may ask women to cover their hair, and some keep scarves at the door. Speak softly. And don't walk directly in front of someone who's praying; wait, or go around behind them. None of it is a test. It's the same thing you do at grandma's: you come in gently.
screen: `SHOES OFF: FACES GO ON THIS FLOOR.` · `THE RIGHT FOOT FIRST.` · `OPEN FOR ME THE DOORS OF YOUR MERCY.` · `DON'T CROSS IN FRONT OF SOMEONE PRAYING.` · then, large: `COME IN GENTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enter a room slowly. Stand up, and walk to the nearest doorway. If you're wearing shoes and it's easy, slip them off. Pause at the threshold. Take one breath. Then step through with your right foot first, and let the left follow. If you pray, you can say, as you step, Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik. If not, just notice the change: the air, the floor, the sound. Then sit down in the new room, and stay still. The bell holds the time.
Shoes off. The first step into a mosque: shoes at the door, the right foot first, and a request for the doors of mercy. Today's word.
Your line: come in gently. Every time you walk into a room today, a kitchen, an office, a meeting, pause at the door for one breath before you step in. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

139.title: Why hijab?
139.hook: women who tore their wraps to cover the same day; in the Qur'an hijab means a curtain, and modesty is asked of men first
139.howItsDone: Many Muslim women cover their hair in front of men outside close family, in many styles and starting at different points in life; men are asked to lower the gaze and dress modestly too, and mosques often ask visitors to dress modestly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shoes off, right foot in, and a few manners for a first visit. Your line was come in gently. Some mosques keep a basket of scarves by the door. Today, the scarf itself. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

Medina. A verse has just come down, and the women who hear it don't wait for the market to open. Aisha remembered it years later, in a report in Bukhari: they took their outer wraps, tore them, and covered themselves with the cloth. Centuries on, the scarf is everywhere: on a goalkeeper, a judge, a girl in a school hallway. So is the question people ask about it, from outside and from inside: why? Today: hijab.
screen: `A VERSE COMES DOWN.` → `THEY TEAR THEIR WRAPS.` → `CENTURIES ON: WHY?`

segments.voice: Start with the word, because it surprises people. In the Qur'an, hijab doesn't mean a scarf. It means a screen or a curtain, something between two spaces. The verse about covering uses another word: khimar, a head covering. Surah an-Nur asks believing women, in Pickthall's words, “to draw their veils over their bosoms.” But read the verse just before it. Before the women are addressed, the men are: “Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest.” In the Qur'an's order, modesty starts with men. Scholars set a minimum covering for men too, and a hadith calls haya', modesty of the whole self, a branch of faith. Then the ruling. Most scholars, past and present, Sunni and Shia, hold that adult women cover their hair in front of men outside close family. Some modern scholars read the verses differently. And within the majority view, the ways are many: a loose shayla, a pinned wrap, a turban style, a chador, and for some women a face veil, which scholars differ about. The journeys are many too. Some girls start young. Some women start at college, or after a hard year, or after Hajj. Some take it off and later put it back on. Many Muslim teachers say a scarf is not a scoreboard for anyone's whole faith. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that Allah does not look at your forms or your wealth, but at your hearts and your deeds. So the lesson isn't about watching women. It's dignity: a modesty asked of both, and no one shamed for where they are on the way.
screen: `IN THE QUR'AN, HIJAB MEANS A CURTAIN.` · `LOWER THE GAZE: SAID TO MEN FIRST.` · `MOST SCHOLARS: COVER. MANY WAYS.` · `HEARTS AND DEEDS, NOT FORMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lower the gaze, kindly. Sit, and breathe. Picture the faces you'll pass today: on a train, in a hallway, on a screen. Notice how fast the eyes judge: clothes, hair, a scarf or no scarf. On each breath out, let that judgment soften, and let your eyes lower a little, the way the verse asks of everyone. Whatever you wear, picture meeting each face as a person, not a verdict. The bell holds the time.
Hijab. In the Qur'an, a screen or curtain; in everyday speech, the head covering many Muslim women wear; and a modesty asked of men and women both. Today's word.
Your line: dignity, not blame. Modesty is asked of both, and nobody is shamed on the way. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

140.title: Mihrab and minbar
140.hook: the niche shows the qiblah; the steps are where the Friday sermon is given
140.howItsDone: In the mosque the imam leads the prayer standing before the mihrab, the niche marking the qiblah, and gives the Friday sermon from the minbar, a stepped pulpit beside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hijab, which in the Qur'an means a curtain, and a modesty asked of men first. Your line was dignity, not blame. Day one hundred forty.

You've washed. Shoes are off. You step into the prayer hall, and the first surprise is how empty it is. No pews. No altar. No statues. Mostly carpet, often with lines woven into it. But look at the far wall. There's a curved niche set into it, sometimes plain, sometimes covered in tiles and calligraphy. And beside it, a small staircase that leads nowhere, with a little platform at the top. Two pieces of furniture in a nearly empty room. Each has a job. Today: mihrab and minbar.
screen: `NO PEWS, NO ALTAR, NO STATUES.` → `A CURVED NICHE IN THE WALL.` → `STAIRS THAT LEAD NOWHERE.`

segments.voice: The niche is the mihrab. Its job is simple: it marks the qiblah, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which you met on day ninety-nine. Find the mihrab in a mosque, and you know which way everyone will face. The imam who leads the prayer stands in front of it. The word itself is in the Qur'an. The Qur'an uses it in the story of Maryam, the mother of Isa: whenever Zakariyya came to her in the mihrab, her place of prayer, he found food with her, and asked where it came from. There it means a place of prayer, a sanctuary, not a niche in a wall. The staircase is the minbar, the pulpit, where the imam gives the sermon at the Friday prayer. Bukhari tells a tender story about it. At first, the Prophet ﷺ gave his sermons standing by the trunk of a palm tree. Then a wooden minbar was made for him. One Friday, when he climbed it, the companions heard the old palm trunk cry out like a child; another report says like a she-camel. The Prophet came down, and put his hand on it, and held it until it went quiet. The mihrab says where to face. The minbar says who will speak. Neither is an altar. What they do together is point a whole room one way, so that the rich man and the cleaner, the old and the new, face the same way.
screen: `MIHRAB — THE NICHE THAT SHOWS THE QIBLAH.` · `MARYAM IN THE MIHRAB.` · `MINBAR — THE STEPS FOR THE SERMON.` · `THE PALM TRUNK THAT CRIED.` · then, large: `EVERYONE FACES THE SAME WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where a room points. Look around the room you're in. Every room faces somewhere: toward a screen, a window, a desk, a door. Where do the chairs point? Where does your body turn by default? Now, if you know it, turn to face the direction of Mecca, or just toward a window, somewhere with light. Sit, and let your whole body face one way. If other people are near, notice that you could all be facing the same way without saying a word. The bell holds the time.
Mihrab. The niche in a mosque's front wall that shows the qiblah, the direction everyone faces in prayer. Today's word.

Your line: everyone faces the same way. Once today, in a line, a meeting or a crowd, notice that you're all facing the same way, and let that make you a little kinder to the person beside you. Day one hundred forty.
